extracted.intended_audience: general readers, journalists, legal researchers and policy analysts interested in Russian media and information law
extracted.subtask_description: Extract and summarize the legal standards and enforcement rules set by the pair of 2019 Russian federal laws (No.31‑FZ and No.27‑FZ) that regulate 'unreliable information' and penalties for its dissemination online. Focus is on prohibitions, enforcement powers, removal obligations, and administrative sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on dissemination of 'unreliable information'
rubrics_metrics.description: The Federal Law of 18 March 2019 No.31-FZ prohibits the dissemination of an "unreliable information" endangering life and/or health of individuals, and/or property, creating the risk of massive violation of public order and/or public security, or the risk of interference with the functioning of vital, transport, social infrastructure, power, industrial and communication facilities, banks and other financial institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This text (Law No.31-FZ) defines the substantive trigger for enforcement: dissemination that either (a) endangers life/health/property, (b) creates risk of large-scale public order or security violations, or (c) risks interference with key infrastructure and financial institutions. The law frames liability around these Concrete categories of harm rather than an abstract 'falsehood' label.

rubrics_metrics.name: Roskomnadzor's authority to designate and extrajudicially block
rubrics_metrics.description: Law No.31-FZ allows the Federal Service for Supervision of Communications, Information Technology and Mass Media (Roskomnadzor) to extrajudicially block access to online media publishing information considered "unreliable" by Russian authorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enforcement is administrative and can be implemented by Roskomnadzor without a judicial order: when Roskomnadzor designates information as 'unreliable' it can order removal and, for non-compliance, block access to the media's website. The law thus vests a regulatory agency with direct takedown/blocking powers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation of online media to remove designated 'unreliable' information immediately
rubrics_metrics.description: According to the laws, an online media is obliged to remove from its website the information designated as "unreliable" by Roskomnadzor immediately after receiving the relevant notification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The removal duty is immediate upon receipt of Roskomnadzor's notification. Failure to comply is a trigger for blocking. This creates a strict notice-and-takedown-style obligation on online publishers operating in Russia.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative fines and sanctions for dissemination (Law No.27-FZ / Code art. 13.15 parts 9–11)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Federal Law of 18 March 2019 No.27-FZ supplemented article 13.15 of the Code of the Russian Federation on Administrative Offenses with parts 9, 10 and 11 providing huge administrative fines for natural persons and juridical persons for the dissemination of "unreliable information".
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Law No.27-FZ implements monetary administrative penalties (large fines) for individuals and legal entities that disseminate information designated as unreliable; the sanctions are codified by adding parts to article 13.15 of the Administrative Offenses Code.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative liability can apply even after compliance/removal
rubrics_metrics.description: Administrative responsibility is incurred even in the case of compliance with the obligation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if an online media removes the designated information immediately following Roskomnadzor's notification, administrative penalties may still be imposed. Compliance with a removal notice does not preclude subsequent fines or other administrative action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of harms/categories that trigger the regime
rubrics_metrics.description: The law targets dissemination that: (a) endangers life and/or health of individuals and/or property; (b) creates the risk of massive violation of public order and/or public security; (c) creates the risk of interference with the functioning of vital, transport, social infrastructure, power, industrial and communication facilities, banks and other financial institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These enumerated categories function as the operative definition for when information is considered sufficiently harmful to be labeled 'unreliable' under the statute; enforcement decisions hinge on whether the published content falls within these risk-based categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entities and examples of enforcement (application of the law)
rubrics_metrics.description: The laws have been applied to individuals and media outlets — first cases cited include an April 2019 case against Arkhangelsk resident Elena Kalinina and administrative fines against Publishing House "Moment Istiny" and its editor-in-chief Evgeniy Gneushev.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reported examples show the law has been used against both private individuals and publishing organizations; courts have sometimes overturned or remanded decisions, but magistrate courts have also reimposed fines. These cases illustrate how the statutory powers and penalties have been operationalized in practice.
